analysis.one_liner: Strips federal endangered-species protection from the polar bear.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died after being referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in January 2011 with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Fish and Wildlife Service's 2008 decision to list the polar bear as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act. A threatened listing triggers protections for the bear's habitat and restricts activities that harm it, including import of sport-hunted polar bear trophies and development that degrades the bear's range. The bill was one sentence long: it declared the listing to have no force or effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries and interests that want fewer Endangered Species Act limits in the Arctic: oil and gas developers whose projects can face habitat reviews, and hunters or dealers who profit from polar bear trophy imports. More broadly, it would benefit anyone seeking to avoid the environmental review that a threatened listing triggers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill nullified the 2008 threatened listing entirely, declaring it to have no force or effect, which would remove all Endangered Species Act protections for the polar bear in one stroke. [S2] [S3]

Delisting would remove the legal barrier the listing creates for activities that harm the bear or its habitat, since a threatened listing restricts actions that jeopardize the species and its range. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on the polar bear, which would lose its federal threatened-species protections, and on the public, whose stake in protecting an imperiled species and its habitat is carried by the Endangered Species Act. The bear's chief threat, the loss of its sea-ice habitat, is a public trust concern; the listing is the main federal tool for addressing it.
analysis.who_pays_short: The polar bear and the public

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove the primary federal legal protection for a species whose habitat is shrinking, without any finding that the bear no longer needs protection. [S2]

Even supporters of limited Endangered Species Act use generally prefer species-by-species scientific review; a one-sentence bill nullifying a specific listing sets a precedent that Congress can override scientists' determinations with a single line of law. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a narrow benefit — fewer federal restrictions on Arctic development and trophy imports — at the cost of eliminating the main federal protection for a species facing habitat loss. It carried no analysis of the bear's status and no replacement protections, so the trade ran almost entirely against conservation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the new Congress and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the Polar Bear Delisting Act on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress. [S1] [S5]
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, which held jurisdiction over Endangered Species Act legislation. [S5]
The bill attracted no cosponsors at any point. [S4]
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The polar bear's threatened listing and the habitat protections that come with it remained in place. Interests hoping to see the Endangered Species Act pared back in the Arctic got nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 112th Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee or scheduled any action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so its support never got large enough to show a party pattern.

industries.industry: Oil and gas development in Alaska and the Arctic
industries.note: The bill would have removed the endangered-species listing that triggers habitat reviews for Arctic development, clearing a legal obstacle for drillers. The bill died, so the habitat protections stand.
A threatened listing restricts trade in polar bear parts, including sport-hunted trophies; delisting would have eased those limits. The bill never advanced.
